exp.0:1:
God is described here as jealous, meaning he will not share his place with others and defends what belongs to him. He is also called the one who takes vengeance: someone who brings justice against evil. The Lord is full of wrath toward evil, which means he has the authority to judge. Keeping anger means that he does not forget the wickedness of those who oppose him.

Nahum writes a prophecy against Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, an empire known for its violence against other peoples. The prophet begins by speaking about the character of God before announcing judgment. The verse that follows clarifies that God is slow to anger, but he does not leave the guilty unpunished.

For today: you can trust that God sees injustice and does not overlook it. That allows you to leave vengeance in his hands, to forgive, and to live in peace without repaying evil with evil.
exp.0:3:
This verse says that God has power over nature. Bashan, Carmel and Lebanon were regions famous for their pastures, forests and flowers, and here it is described how they wither before God.

The prophet Nahum speaks on God's behalf against Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, which had oppressed many peoples. He describes God's power to show that no human power can resist him. For the people of Judah, this was a comfort: God sees injustice and does not let it pass.

For today: when you feel that evil or the powerful have the last word, remember that God is greater. Rest in him and trust his justice, without taking revenge on your own.
exp.0:4:
When God appears, the whole of creation reacts with fear. The mountains tremble, the hills melt away, and the earth is shaken, or burns, as the Hebrew word can be understood in several ways. No one is left out: the world and all who live in it feel his presence.

Nahum is a prophet who announces God's judgment on Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, known for its violence. He speaks to an oppressed people to remind them that God is patient, but does not leave wickedness unpunished. These poetic images show his absolute power.

Today we can take God's justice seriously without living in fear. Verse 7 says that he is a refuge for those who trust in him. If something troubles you or seems unfair, entrust it to God with confidence.
exp.0:9:
They say that God's enemies, even when they seem strong, will be destroyed. They are tangled together like woven thorns, and they are like drunkards who cannot see the danger. Dry stubble is the dried residue of flax or hemp, which catches fire very easily. In the same way they will be burned up, unable to resist. The Hebrew text is difficult, and some translators understand the images a little differently.

The prophet Nahum speaks in God's name against Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, which had oppressed many peoples, including Judah. The verses nearby speak of someone who planned evil against God. The message comforted Judah: God does not overlook injustice.

For today: if you see that wickedness seems to be winning, do not grow bitter or take revenge. Trust that God is just and acts in his own time. In the meantime, keep doing good and take refuge in him.
exp.0:14:
Upon the mountains appears a messenger who brings good news and announces peace. Judah is invited to celebrate its feasts and fulfill its vows, that is, the promises made to God, because the wicked will no longer invade them. He has been completely destroyed.

God speaks through the prophet Nahum. He announces the fall of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, which had oppressed Judah. The heavy burdens that once weighed on Judah stand as symbols of that oppression. Scholars debate the exact date, but the message brings comfort to a people weary of suffering.

For today: when you go through a situation that seems endless, remember that God sees the injustice and has the final word. While you wait, return to worshiping him and keep what you promised him.
exp.1:2:
This verse describes an army advancing with an impressive appearance. Their shields are red, and the soldiers are dressed in scarlet, a deep red dye. The chariots flash like polished metal that gleams like flames. The phrase about the fir trees is difficult: some translators understand them to be wooden spears that are shaken, and others think of cypress trees or of soldiers trembling. There are several interpretations.

The prophet Nahum announces God's judgment against Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, a cruel empire that had oppressed Israel. The army that comes against it is the instrument of divine judgment. God promises to restore his people, even though they have been plundered.

For today: even when evil seems to hold power for a long time, God does not forget it. We can rest in the knowledge that he does justice and cares for his own, and in the meantime keep trusting and doing good.
exp.1:9:
She is empty, emptied out, and in ruins. Its people feel their hearts melt in fear, lose all their courage. Their knees tremble and knock together, they feel pain in their waist and back, and their faces turn pale or gloomy from anguish. Some translators understand that the faces grow dark, and others that they turn ashen; the original is difficult.

Here the prophet Nahum speaks, announcing God's judgment on Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, known for its violence and its plundering. The text describes the city already conquered and its soldiers looting its riches. The words that follow compare Assyria to a lion that devoured other peoples.

For today: power and riches gained through injustice are not secure. Let us ask God to help us live with justice and to trust in Him, not in what we accumulate.
exp.1:12:
God speaks to Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, and tells her that he is against her. He will burn her war chariots until they turn to smoke, the sword will destroy her young lions (her young warriors), and he will take away from the earth the plunder she stole. The messengers who carried her orders and threats will be heard no more.

The LORD of hosts speaks through the prophet Nahum. Assyria was a very violent empire that had oppressed many peoples, and the lion was an image of its power and its plundering. God announces that this power will come to an end. Many place this message shortly before the fall of Nineveh, around 612 BC, although the exact date of the writing is debated.

For today: God sees injustice and does not forget it. We can rest in the fact that he is a just judge, and ask him to keep us from using our power to take advantage of others.
exp.2:1:
This verse describes the arrival of an army through its sounds: the crack of the whip, the rumble of the wheels, galloping horses, and chariots bounding over the ground. The picture is of an army that rushes forward with great force and tramples everything in its path.

The prophet Nahum announces God's judgment on Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, a city known for its violence, its lies, and its plundering of other peoples (3:1). For this reason he paints the scene of its fall as if he were already seeing it. Scholars understand the noise to be that of the invading army that would come against the city.

For today: God does not ignore injustice or the abuse of power, even when they seem to last a long time. This is a comfort if we suffer oppression, and it invites us to examine whether there is deceit or abuse in our work, our business, or our dealings with others, and to seek to live with honesty.
exp.2:7:
God asks Nineveh whether she is any better than No-amon, a great city that seemed impossible to conquer. It was surrounded by rivers and waters, and the water was like its wall.

The prophet Nahum speaks on behalf of God against Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, known for its violence. No-amon is usually identified with Thebes in Egypt, which fell to Assyria around 663 B.C. If Thebes, so well protected, was defeated, Nineveh had no reason to believe itself safe.

For today: let us not trust in our defenses, such as money, success, or position, to feel secure. All of these can fail. Let us live with humility and seek our security in God, who is just and faithful.
exp.2:8:
It speaks of the city of No-amon (the ancient Thebes of Egypt) as having great strength. Ethiopia was its power, Egypt had no limit to its resources, and Put and Libya, neighboring peoples, were its helpers. "Strength" here means might or support, and "Put" is usually linked to a region in North Africa.

The prophet Nahum speaks to Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, and announces judgment for its violence and cruelty. He reminds her that No-amon, though it seemed invincible and had allies, still fell into captivity, probably at the hands of the Assyrians themselves. The message is: if she fell, Nineveh can also fall.

For today: let us not place our ultimate security in money, power, or good connections. All of those can fail. God is the only firm refuge, so it is wise to live with humility and trust in Him.
exp.2:12:
Here God tells Nineveh that its soldiers, its fighting men, will become weak and afraid, like frightened people in the midst of battle. The gates of the land will be thrown wide open, that is, left completely open to the enemy. Fire will destroy the bars that secured the city's gates.

The prophet Nahum announces, on God's behalf, judgment against Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, known for its violence and cruelty. The passage compares its fall to that of another city already defeated, Thebes. The strongholds that seemed secure will fall easily, like ripe figs.

For today: do not put your security in your strength, your money, or your achievements, because none of these will hold forever. Seek refuge in God, who is just and faithful, and live with humility.
exp.2:13:
It says that Nineveh should prepare for a siege: that it should draw water for the siege, strengthen its walls and fortresses, tread the clay to make bricks, and repair the kiln where they were baked. The siege is the enemy's attack on the city. It is an order full of irony: prepare yourself as much as you like.

The prophet Nahum speaks, delivering a message from God against Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, known for its violence and cruelty. The following verses announce that, despite all these preparations, fire and the sword would destroy it. Nahum shows that no human power can stop the judgment of God.

For today: do not place your security in your resources, plans, or achievements, because they can fail. Do what is yours to do with wisdom, but rest in God, who is just and is a firm refuge (Nahum 1:7).
exp.1:11:
The lion mauled enough prey to feed his cubs and the lioness. "Strangled" means that he killed his victims by choking them. "Filled" means that he packed his dens and lairs with the kill he had taken. In this way, his caves were stocked with what he had stolen.

The prophet Nahum speaks against Nineveh, the capital of Assyria. He uses the image of the lion to describe a violent empire that plundered other peoples. But the question that comes before it already announces its ruin: where is that lion's den now? Right after that, God himself says: "Behold, I am against you." His power had a limit, and God would judge it.

For today: do not envy or imitate those who prosper by abusing others. What is gained through injustice does not last. Trust that God sees everything and does justice in his own time, and seek to live with honesty and compassion.
exp.2:18:
It says that Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, has an injury that cannot be healed. Here "injury" means a fracture or a deadly blow, and the wound has grown worse and no longer heals. The picture of people applauding means they cheer with joy at seeing her fall. The closing question points out that Assyria's cruelty reached nearly everyone, again and again.

The prophet Nahum speaks in God's name and announces judgment on Nineveh. Assyria was an empire known for its cruelty, and it had oppressed many peoples, including Israel. The verses before this one describe how its leaders will disappear and its people will be scattered. The book brings comfort to the oppressed: God does not ignore injustice.

For today: if you suffer from an injustice, trust that God sees it and will judge with justice. And if you have power, remember that abusing others has consequences. Use your influence to serve and to care for others, not to harm them.
exp.2:15:
It says Nineveh had a huge number of merchants, more than the stars of the sky. But the young locust strips the land bare and then flies away. In other words, that wealth could not protect the city; it vanished quickly, like a swarm that arrives, destroys everything, and leaves.

The prophet Nahum speaks here, announcing God's judgment against Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, a city famous for its violence and power. Scholars do not fully agree on whether the young locust refers to the merchants who flee when they sense danger or to the invaders who plunder. In either case, the message is that its prosperity would not save it.

For today: money, business, and success can disappear all at once. It is worth working honestly, but we should place our trust in God, who does endure.
exp.0:12:
God tells Judah that he will break the yoke that weighs on its neck and tear away its shackles. A "yoke" is the wooden frame placed over the necks of working animals; here it stands for slavery and the weight of foreign rule. The "shackles" are the bonds that held that yoke and the people beneath it in place.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Nahum. The message is addressed to Judah, which was suffering under the power of Assyria, and which is described as the afflicted people. God announces that this oppressor will be destroyed. Nahum does not say exactly who the wicked counselor is, and scholars interpret this in different ways.

For today: if you are carrying oppression, fear, or a bond that seems endless, remember that God sees and has the final word. Pray with confidence, seek help, and wait on Him, knowing that his justice and his deliverance come in his time.
exp.2:2:
This verse paints a scene of war: charging horsemen, swords and spears flashing, and heaps of dead bodies everywhere. There are so many corpses that they cannot be counted, and those who flee stumble over the dead.

Nahum prophesies against Nineveh, capital of the Assyrian empire, called a "city of bloodshed" because of its violence, its lies, and its plundering. The prophet announces that God, the Lord of hosts, will judge her. Many understand this passage to describe the attack that would fall upon her, though not everyone agrees on the historical details of how it happened.

For today: violence and deceit are not a good foundation for any life or any society. God sees injustice and does not leave it without a response. We can trust that he will do justice, and in the meantime, choose truth and honesty in our everyday lives.
exp.2:3:
Nineveh was facing ruin because of her many harlotries, meaning her unfaithfulness and immorality. She is pictured as a prostitute who is alluring and seductive. She is also the seductive mistress of sorcery: she uses deception and spells to draw others in. Her sorcery and her prostitution both serve to betray nations and clans, seducing and enslaving them so that she can profit from them.

The prophet Nahum speaks, passing on God's message against Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, an empire known for its violence. Many understand the image as a picture of its idolatry, its political seduction, and its exploitation of other peoples. God announces that he will not overlook that wickedness and that he will judge it.

For today: do not let yourself be dazzled by power or success that rests on deception and injustice. Seek to live with honesty, and trust that God sees and judges with justice.
exp.1:4:
He summons his nobles, and they stumble as they advance. They race to the city wall, and the protective shield is set in place. This verse says the king of Nineveh will call his strongest soldiers to action, but they will stumble in their haste and fear. They will rush toward the city wall to defend it, and the protective shield will be set in place to guard the wall. Some scholars understand this shield to be a siege engine; others, a defense of the besieged. The text does not allow us to be certain.

Here the prophet Nahum speaks, announcing God's judgment against Nineveh, capital of Assyria, famous for its cruelty. The chapter describes the enemy attack and the disorder of the defenders. God shows that no human power is eternal.

For today: do not place your security in your strength, your money, or your plans. When everything seems firm, remember that only God truly sustains. Seek refuge in Him and live with humility and justice.
exp.2:9:
Nahum describes what befell the city of No-amon, which seemed impossible to conquer, and says it too was carried into exile. Her little children were "dashed in pieces," that is, beaten violently to death, at the head of every street. Over her dignitaries they cast lots, as one divides spoil, and her nobles were bound in chains.

God speaks through the prophet Nahum to Nineveh, the capital of Assyria. He reminds her that No-amon, the great Egyptian city also known as Thebes, had rivers, allies and walls, and yet it fell. Many understand that this refers to its fall before Assyria, and that now Nineveh would suffer the same.

For today: do not trust in your power, your money or your security as if they were eternal. Rest in God, who is just and rules over every empire.
exp.1:7:
Nineveh has been like a pool of water for as long as it has stood, full of people and plenty. But now its strength is draining away, and its people are running. Someone cries, "Stop! Stop!", but no one turns back.

The prophet Nahum announces God's judgment on Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, an empire known for its violence. He speaks to Judah to bring comfort: the oppressor will fall. The "gates of the rivers" probably refer to the floodgates or channels of the city. Some think the pool speaks of its numerous people; others, of its wealth and security.

For today: no force, wealth, or fame is so firm that it does not depend on God. We can rest in the fact that he is just, and place our security in him, not in what we have.
exp.0:0:
This is a solemn message against the city of Nineveh. The word "burden" here means a heavy message, a declaration of judgment. The word "vision" shows that God revealed this message to the prophet. Nahum is identified as "the Elkoshite," which probably tells us where he or his family came from, though the exact location is not known with certainty.

Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, an empire known for its cruelty and for oppressing many nations, including Israel. The speaker is the prophet, who passes on what God showed him. Years earlier, Nineveh had turned from its sins when Jonah preached to it, but later the city returned to its wickedness. Scholars date the book to different times, but all agree it was written before Nineveh fell.

For today: God sees injustice and does not ignore it. If you are worn down by seeing evil, trust that God is just, and leave in his hands what you cannot set right.
exp.1:3:
The chariots dash through the streets and rush around the squares of the city, flashing like torches and darting about like lightning. The picture is one of great violence and speed. The verse's own words describe the chariots rushing around the plazas and darting about, which means they race forward with force and move quickly back and forth through the open spaces of the city.

The prophet Nahum announces, on behalf of God, the fall of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, a cruel nation that oppressed many peoples. Many understand that the army he describes is the one that attacks the city, though some think it refers to its defenders in the chaos. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: God sees injustice and does not overlook it. If you suffer abuse or see power misused, trust that God is just, and examine whether you yourself are trusting in your own strength.
exp.0:5:
It says that no one can withstand the anger of God. The questions "who can withstand His indignation?" and "who can endure His burning anger?" are rhetorical: the answer is no one. "Burning anger" speaks of a very intense anger. His wrath is "poured out like fire," and even rocks are shattered before Him.

Nahum is a prophet who announces God's judgment on Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, famous for its cruelty. Earlier, God had shown compassion to that city (as in Jonah), but now it had returned to violence. The prophet describes God's power over nature to show that no empire can stop Him. The next verse gives comfort to those who trust in Him.

For today: do not take God's justice lightly, but do not live in fear if you trust in Him. He is good and knows His own. You can leave in His hands the injustices that hurt you and seek refuge in Him.
exp.0:7:
He says that God will bring a complete end to the place of his enemies, like a flood that sweeps away everything in its path. The phrase "make an end" means he will destroy completely, leaving nothing behind. The "place" most likely refers to the enemy's city, that is, Nineveh. And the "darkness" that pursues his enemies speaks of judgment, ruin, and no way of escape.

Here the prophet Nahum speaks, announcing a message against Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, a cruel empire that oppressed other peoples. The verses before this one show God as a powerful judge, but also as a refuge for those who trust in him. Some scholars see the "flood" as a symbolic image; others connect it with a real rise of the river during the fall of Nineveh. It is not certain what the exact detail was.

For today: if you see injustice, do not despair. Trust that God rules and judges with justice; in the meantime, take refuge in him and live with humility.
exp.1:10:
This verse is a question full of irony: "Where is the lions' lair?" The "feeding ground" is the place where the young lions are fed, and "with nothing to frighten them away" means that nothing stood in their way or made them afraid. Before, the lion and lioness and their cubs roamed freely, with no fear of anyone. Now that place no longer exists.

The prophet Nahum speaks of the fall of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria. Assyria was known for its violence, and for that reason it is compared to a lion that plunders and destroys. God himself declares that he is against it. Many understand the question as a mocking lament over a power that seemed invincible.

For today: do not trust in power, money, or human strength, because none of these lasts forever. Rest in God, who is just and rules over every nation.
exp.0:8:
It says that making plans against God is useless. The question "Whatever you plot against the LORD?" is like asking: "What are you scheming to do?" "Bring to an end" means to finish something completely, to destroy it totally. "Affliction will not rise up a second time" can be understood in this way: the suffering that Nineveh caused will not happen again, or God will put an end to evil once and for all, without needing to repeat it. Scholars interpret it in both ways.

The prophet Nahum speaks to Judah, which had suffered under the power of Assyria, and also addresses Nineveh, its capital. He reminds them that God protects those who trust in him, but that he will not allow wickedness to go unanswered.

For today: when injustice or distress seem enormous to you, trust that God knows your situation and has the final word. Instead of living in fear, rest in him and do not use your strength to oppose what he wants.
exp.0:2:
God is slow to anger and great in power, and he will by no means leave the guilty unpunished. The idea of slowness is part of the same picture: he holds back his anger, yet that patience does not mean he is indifferent to wrong. The storm described here is a powerful one, with wind and whirlwind moving across the sky. The clouds are like the dust raised by his feet as he walks, an image of his majesty and greatness.

Nahum is the prophet who speaks. He writes about Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, an empire known for its violence against other peoples. The message reminded Judah that God sees injustice and will respond to it. His patience is not weakness; it is mercy that gives time, but that time has a limit.

For today: if someone has hurt you, you can trust that God is just, so you do not need to take revenge yourself. And if you have failed, do not take advantage of his patience. Come to him today and ask for forgiveness.
exp.1:0:
This verse says that an enemy who scatters and destroys is coming against the city. Because of this, the verse gives its commands with irony: guard the fortress, watch the road, brace yourselves, and summon all your strength. Nineveh is told to prepare for battle, though the preparation cannot save it.

The prophet Nahum speaks to Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, a city known for its violence. Scholars often see a mockery here: however much the city prepares, it will not be able to stop the judgment. The verses that follow show that God cares for his people and brings an end to oppression. The exact date of Nineveh's fall is generally placed in the seventh century B.C., although the details are debated.

For today: do not trust in your own defenses, your money, or your power to feel safe. Injustice will not last forever, and God remains the refuge of those who trust in him. Seek your security in God today and live with justice.
exp.1:5:
It says that the river gates, the water entrances that guarded the city, will be thrown open, and that the king's palace will collapse. "Collapses" in this verse means it falls apart and is undone. The "river gates" may be the floodgates that controlled the water, or the openings through which the rivers flowed into the city.

The prophet Nahum announces God's judgment against Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, famous for its violence and cruelty. The verses before this one describe the attack of an enemy army. Some believe this verse speaks of a flood that weakened the defenses, but it is not known with certainty how it happened. What is clear is that what seemed secure fell.

For today: no human power, however great it may seem, is above God. Trust in Him, not in your own securities, and live with justice and humility.
exp.0:13:
God speaks to Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, and declares that its family line and its name will come to an end, with no descendants to carry it on. To "cut off" means to destroy or cut down. God will remove the carved idols and cast images from the house of its gods, and that same place will become its grave. The reason given is that Nineveh is "contemptible," meaning it is despicable because of its wickedness.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Nahum. Assyria had oppressed Judah and other peoples harshly. The verses nearby announce freedom for Judah: the oppressing yoke will be broken. This verse shows that God judges the oppressor and that idols cannot save anyone.

For today: God sees injustice and does not leave it forever. If you are suffering today or see abuse, trust that He is just and cares for His own. And do not place your security in things that cannot save.
exp.2:11:
It says that Nineveh's fortresses, which seemed so secure, would be like fig trees with the first ripe figs. The first ripe figs are the earliest figs of the season, very ripe and soft. A single shake is enough to make them fall straight into the mouth of the one who wants to eat them. In other words, the city would give way almost without resistance.

Here the prophet Nahum speaks, announcing God's judgment on Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, known for its violence and cruelty. He had earlier mentioned that another city, called No-Amon, also fell, and he warns that Nineveh will suffer the same fate. Its fortifications, then, would not save it. The message comforted an oppressed people: God does not ignore injustice.

For today: do not place your ultimate security in your defenses, your money, or your success, because they can fall easily. Trust in God, who is just and steadfast, and live in a humble and upright way.
exp.2:16:
The verse says that the leaders and guards of Nineveh, who seem so numerous and powerful, will be like swarming locusts. They settle on the walls on a cold day, but when the sun rises they fly away, and no one knows where they have gone. The phrase "your guards" refers to the officials or high leaders, and "your scribes" refers to the record-keepers and officials who served the city.

The prophet Nahum speaks on behalf of God and announces judgment on Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, known for its violence and cruelty. Its leaders seemed firm, but when the time comes, they will flee and disappear. Scholars understand the image in different ways, but all see a sudden and complete fall.

For today: human power, prestige, and the number of followers are not a secure foundation. Trust more in God, who is just and endures, than in any passing force of this world.
exp.1:8:
This verse is a command spoken to the invaders of Nineveh: "Plunder the silver! Plunder the gold!" It says there is no end to the treasure, an abundance of every precious thing. The city's wealth seems endless, and the command makes clear that it will be taken away.

Here the prophet Nahum speaks, announcing God's judgment on Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, a city known for its violence and its power. The prophet describes its fall as though it were already happening. The riches it gathered, largely at the expense of other peoples, now pass into the hands of its enemies.

For today: riches may seem lasting, but they are not secure. It is worth asking ourselves what we truly trust in, and seeking with simplicity what cannot be lost: a righteous life and trust in God.
exp.0:6:
The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of distress; He cares for those who trust in Him. "Stronghold" means a safe place, like a fortified wall. "Cares for" does not mean only knowing who they are, but looking after them and staying close to them.

The prophet Nahum speaks to Judah, which was suffering under the power of Assyria, whose center was Nineveh. Before this verse, he describes the power and anger of God against evil. Afterward, he announces that God will put an end to the enemies of his people. This verse is a breath of relief in the midst of judgment: the same God who is dreadful to the oppressors is a refuge for those who trust in him.

When you are going through a difficult moment, do not carry everything alone. Speak to God honestly and trust that he sees you and takes care of you, even when you do not understand everything that is happening.
exp.2:14:
It says that Nineveh, even with its defenses, will be destroyed. The fire will consume it and the sword will cut it down, just as the young locust strips the crops bare. Then there is an ironic command: "make yourself many like the young locust." In other words, even if you are a great multitude, that will not save you.

The prophet Nahum speaks, announcing a judgment of God against Nineveh, the capital of the Assyrian empire. It was a city famous for its violence and its pride. The prophet mocks its preparations: repairing walls, gathering water, and making bricks. None of that will stop what God has already decided.

For today: do not place your security in your strength, your money, or your plans. All of that can fail. Trust in God, who is just and cares for those who take refuge in Him.
exp.0:10:
Nahum 1:11 speaks of someone who comes out of Nineveh and plots evil against the LORD. The Hebrew idea behind "plotter of evil" is a person who schemes or devises wickedness. The one described is a counselor of wickedness, a man who gives twisted plans and evil advice. The text does not name him. Some readers think it points to an Assyrian king or leader, perhaps Sennacherib, while others take it as a description of Assyria's power in general.

The prophet Nahum speaks here with a message from the LORD. Judah lived under the heavy hand of Assyria. God declares that this power, which dared to stand against him, will be completely destroyed, and that the judgment will not have to be repeated. In this way he comforts his people with the promise of deliverance.

For today, do not lose heart when evil seems to advance with its plans. God sees those who oppose him, and he is never out of control. Rest in the knowledge that he knows when and how to bring justice, and keep trusting him.
exp.2:17:
This verse says that the leaders of Assyria, called "shepherds" and "officers," are asleep, meaning they can no longer act. So the people are scattered across the mountains with no one to gather them. The word "sleep" suggests a rest that in this case means defeat or death.

The prophet Nahum speaks in God's name and announces the fall of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, an empire known for its cruelty toward other peoples. The earlier images, such as the locusts that vanish when the sun rises, show that its power seemed enormous but would disappear. For Judah, it was a message of comfort: God does justice.

For today: do not place your security in human power, however great it may seem. Trust in God, who governs over all authority, and seek to use whatever influence you have justly.
exp.2:5:
God says he will throw filth and refuse at Nineveh, bringing her low and leaving her exposed like rubbish. Repulsive things are what he will hurl at her, disgrace her in front of others, and make her a spectacle, something no one wants to look at or touch.

The Lord of hosts speaks through the prophet Nahum. Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, is described as a prostitute who seduced and dominated the nations through deceit and sorcery. God announces his judgment for her violence and her pride. Her fall would be seen by all the nations.

For today: power, beauty, or success protect no one when they are used to deceive and oppress. God sees injustice and does not overlook it. We can examine whether we use what we have to serve with truth and honesty, and trust that God will bring about justice in his time.
exp.1:6:
The verse says that the city will be carried off into exile. Its people will be marched away, and its women will go with them, moaning like doves and beating their breasts in grief. Some scholars believe the Hebrew word rendered "Huzzab" is a name or an expression that is hard to pin down, so it is understood in several ways.

Nahum announces God's judgment against Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, an empire known for its violence. The prophet speaks in God's name and wants to comfort Judah: the oppressor will not last forever.

For today: no human power, however great it may seem, is above God. If you suffer injustice, trust that He sees and that His justice will come. And if you have power or success, live with humility.
exp.1:1:
This verse says that the LORD will restore to his people, called Jacob and Israel, the splendor they had lost. The reason is that destroyers had laid them waste and ruined the "branches" of their vine, the young growths that stand for what once bore fruit among the people.

Nahum announces the fall of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, an empire that had harmed Israel. The verse before this one is an ironic warning to the enemy who is approaching. Here the prophet speaks on God's behalf and reminds the reader that the punishment of the oppressor is also comfort for the wounded people. Some scholars debate how to understand exactly the phrase "like the splendor of Israel."

For today: if you have suffered losses or injustice, you can trust that God knows how to restore what was damaged. Give Him your pain and wait on Him without taking revenge.
exp.2:0:
Here the verse announces a "woe," that is, a warning of judgment, against a city of blood. "City of blood" means that it was stained by many deaths. "Plunder" and "prey" are goods taken by force and people who are continually preyed upon. The city was full of lies and never stopped abusing others.

The prophet Nahum speaks in the name of God. From the book, almost everyone understands that the city is Nineveh, capital of Assyria, famous for its cruelty toward other peoples. The verses that follow describe an attack with chariots, horses and swords, and many dead. Scholars debate the exact date, but the message is clear: God does not ignore violence.

For today: God sees injustice, even when it seems that no one stops it. You can examine your life honestly: is there any lying or unfair advantage that you find hard to let go of? Ask God for help to live in truth and to treat others with justice and respect.
exp.2:6:
This verse says that those who see Nineveh destroyed will pull back from her in horror. They will say, "Nineveh is devastated." No one will grieve for her. The question "who will grieve for her?" shows that she will have no one to mourn her. The closing question, "Where can I find comforters for you?", shows that no one will be left to console her.

God speaks through the prophet Nahum. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, an empire known for its violence and cruelty. God announces judgment for that wickedness. The following verses compare her with the Egyptian city of No-amon (Thebes), which also fell even though it seemed secure.

For today: power, wealth, or alliances do not shield us from the justice of God. It is worth living with humility and treating others with justice and compassion, trusting that God sees everything and acts with righteousness.
exp.2:4:
God says that he is against Nineveh. "I am against you" means "here I am, standing against you." Lifting your skirts over your face is an image of public humiliation: Nineveh will be exposed, and her nakedness and shame will be shown to all the nations and kingdoms.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Nahum. Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, is compared to a prostitute who deceived and dominated the peoples with her abuses and her power. God responds with justice to so much violence. It is strong and symbolic language, typical of the prophetic poetry of that time.

For today: God sees what lies hidden behind power, fame, or appearance. Today we can live with humility and honesty, without taking advantage of others, trusting that God does justice in his own time.
exp.0:11:
He says that God speaks with authority. Even though the enemies of his people are allied and numerous, they will be cut down, that is, cut off the way grass or a tree is cut down, and they will pass away, meaning they will vanish. Then God speaks directly to Judah: "Though I have afflicted you, I will afflict you no longer." The punishment has a limit.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Nahum. The message is directed against Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, which had oppressed Judah. Many understand that "he that imagineth evil against the LORD" refers to the Assyrian king or his rule, although this is interpreted in several ways. God comforts his afflicted people by promising them deliverance.

For today: when you suffer, or see that evil seems strong and numerous, remember that God governs history. Your trials are not eternal, nor are they outside his care. Trust in Him and wait for his time.
exp.2:10:
Nineveh, the great city of Assyria, is also warned that she will face defeat. The image of being "drunk" does not refer only to wine. In the prophets it often stands for God's judgment, which leaves a person dazed and without strength. Her going into hiding suggests that she will be hidden away or under siege. She will seek refuge, a place of safety, because the enemy will hem her in.

Nahum announces the fall of Nineveh. Before that, the prophet recalls Thebes (No-amon) in Egypt, a city that seemed secure, with allies, and yet was taken into captivity. Nineveh had been cruel to other peoples, and now she is told: "You too." Many believe this was written shortly before her fall in 612 B.C., although the exact date is not certain.

For today: no human power or success makes us untouchable. It is wiser to take refuge in God than to trust our own defenses.

sum.1: Nahum describes how a destroying army attacks Nineveh, and its defenses, its palace, and its riches fall while its people flee in fear. Nineveh is compared to a lion that used to prey on others and believed itself safe. God declares that he is against her and that her violence will come to an end, and he also promises to restore the glory of Jacob.
sum.0: Nahum declares that God is jealous and just: he is slow to anger, but he does not leave the guilty unpunished, and his power shakes the natural world. He is a refuge for those who trust in him, while Nineveh and its wickedness will be destroyed. For Judah there is hope: its oppression will end, and good news of peace is coming.
sum.2: Nahum announces God's judgment against Nineveh, a city full of bloodshed, lies, and violence. God will expose it to shame, and neither its fortresses nor its vast trade will save it, just as they did not save No-amon. Its fall will be complete, and all who suffered from its wickedness will rejoice.
